# Results — Study 641 (Sell in May)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test — **"Sell in
May and go away"** (the Halloween indicator, Bouman & Jacobsen 2002): U.S. equities earn almost
all of their return Nov→Apr ("winter"), so a rational investor holds stocks in winter and sits
in cash May→Oct ("summer"). Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py`
to reproduce every number. As-of **2026-06-30** (the last complete calendar month; the partial
current month is dropped). Fingerprints `f17f1fc81bc9` (^GSPC) / `8324508d6a89` (SPY) /
`02c7f8f5728e` (^SP500TR) / `20827eb9627f` (^IRX).*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily ^GSPC (**price-only**, 19,244 rows, 1950-01-03 → 2026-06-30), SPY (dividend/split-adjusted close, 8,410 rows, 1993-02-01 →), ^SP500TR (genuine total-return index, 9,694 rows, 1988-01-05 →), ^IRX (13-week T-bill discount yield, cash proxy, 16,607 rows, 1960-01-04 →) |
| Calendar | fixed, non-fit partition: **Nov→Apr = winter**, **May→Oct = summer** — known in full years ahead, so no look-ahead is possible in either leg (Bouman & Jacobsen's own definition) |
| Monthly points | ^GSPC **917** (1950-02 → 2026-06), SPY **400** (1993-03 →), ^SP500TR **461** (1988-02 →), ^IRX **798** monthly cash-rate points (1960-01 →) |
| Statistics | Welch *t* for the winter/summer group split (planned primary); **Newey-West (3 lags)** *t* on the winter-dummy regression as the HAC cross-check; a **year-block bootstrap** (10,000 draws, resampling whole Halloween *years*) and an exact **sign test** with a Wilson interval on the paired per-year gap |
| Execution / costs | one documented convention: the Nov→Apr / May→Oct split is a fixed calendar rule known years in advance, so a position is held for the entire named month with **zero look-ahead**; the Halloween timer charges 2 × one-way cost × NAV per switch (2 switches/yr) |
| Data quirks (named) | **^GSPC is price-only** — no dividends — so its long history (1950–) is *not* directly comparable in level terms to the dividend-inclusive SPY/^SP500TR tapes; ^IRX is an annualized discount-yield quote, converted to an approximate monthly cash rate (`yield/100/12`), not a true money-market total return |

No survivorship on the Signal axis: ^GSPC, SPY and ^SP500TR are indices/index-trackers, not
survivor panels.

## The headline — winter (Nov→Apr) vs summer (May→Oct) monthly log return

| tape (sample) | winter %/mo | summer %/mo | gap %/mo | 6-mo cumulative (winter / summer) | Welch *t* | NW(3) *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **^GSPC**, price-only, 1950–2026 (n=459/458) | **+1.048%** | +0.278% | **+0.770%** | +6.49% / +1.68% | **+2.78** | **+2.96** |
| **^SP500TR**, total-return, 1988–2026 (n=231/230) | +1.168% | +0.643% | +0.526% | +7.26% / +3.93% | +1.33 | +1.42 |
| **SPY**, dividend-adjusted, 1993–2026 (n=200/200) | +1.092% | +0.619% | +0.473% | +6.77% / +3.78% | +1.10 | +1.18 |

The deep, **price-only** 76-year tape clears the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar two ways (Welch and HAC).
But the **dividend-inclusive** tapes — the ones that actually describe what a real portfolio
earns — sit at *t* = 1.1–1.3: positive, same direction, but **not certified**. Summer's monthly
mean is **positive** on every tape (never close to zero, let alone negative) — the folklore's
implicit premise ("summer is dead money") is false on its face before any significance test.

## Year-block pairing — one (summer, winter) point per Halloween year

Cumulative log return of each 6-month leg, paired within the same Halloween year (winter(Y) =
Nov(Y)→Apr(Y+1)); resampling entire *years* respects the within-year correlation and never lets
a bootstrap draw straddle a season boundary.

| tape | years | winter wins | hit rate (Wilson 95%) | sign-test *p* | bootstrap mean gap | bootstrap *t* | 95% CI | P(gap ≤ 0) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **^GSPC** (1950–2025) | 76 | 47/76 | **61.8%** [50.6%, 71.9%] | 0.0505 | **+4.64%** | **+3.16** | [+1.78%, +7.56%] | **0.0006** |
| **^SP500TR** (1988–2025) | 38 | 23/38 | 60.5% [44.7%, 74.4%] | 0.2559 | +3.26% | +1.61 | [−0.69%, +7.17%] | 0.0542 |
| SPY (1993–2025) | 33 | 19/33 | 57.6% [40.8%, 72.8%] | 0.4869 | +3.00% | +1.41 | [−1.08%, +7.08%] | 0.0765 |

Same pattern as the headline split: decisive on the deep price-only sample (bootstrap CI clear
of zero, sign-test borderline), **not certified** on the shorter dividend-inclusive samples
(sign-test *p* = 0.26–0.49; bootstrap CIs straddle zero).

## By calendar month — ^GSPC 1950–2026 (mean %, n)

| Jan | Feb | Mar | Apr | May | Jun | Jul | Aug | **Sep** | **Oct** | Nov | Dec |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| +0.96 | −0.10 | +0.89 | +1.45 | +0.37 | +0.12 | +1.22 | −0.06 | **−0.73** | **+0.74** | +1.76 | +1.35 |

September is the *only* calendar month with a negative 76-year mean; October's mean is
positive, but (see below) carries the fattest crash tail of the summer half. Four of the six
"winter" months (Jan, Mar, Apr, Nov, Dec) beat every "summer" month outright — the seasonal
isn't one giant six-month drag, it is concentrated in a few individually weak/volatile months.

## "A handful of bad autumns" — drop the 5 worst Septembers + 5 worst Octobers

| | gap (winter − summer) | Welch *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| Full sample (n=917) | **+0.770%/mo** | **+2.78** |
| After dropping 10 months (1.1% of the sample) | +0.496%/mo | **+1.88** |

Dropped: 1974-09, 1978-10, 1979-10, 1986-09, 1987-10 (Black Monday), 2002-09, 2008-09, 2008-10
(GFC), 2018-10, 2022-09 — ten crash-adjacent autumn months, 1.1% of the 917-month sample.
Removing them shrinks the gap by **35%** and drops the Welch *t* **below the certification bar**
(2.78 → 1.88). A material share of the "deep history clears *t* ≥ 2" result rides on a short list
of well-known bad autumns, not a smooth, broad-based winter tailwind.

## The Halloween timer — long Nov→Apr, cash (^IRX) May→Oct, vs buy & hold

Excess-of-cash Sharpe both legs (a part-time-in-cash timer must not race a raw buy-and-hold
Sharpe); 2 × one-way cost × NAV per switch, 2 switches/yr.

| tape | cost | timer CAGR | buy&hold CAGR | timer excess-Sharpe | b&h excess-Sharpe | timer maxDD | b&h maxDD |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **^SP500TR** (38.4y) | 5 bps | +8.06% | **+10.23%** | 0.52 | **0.54** | −31.7% | −53.2% |
| **^SP500TR** (38.4y) | 10 bps | +7.85% | +10.23% | 0.50 | 0.54 | −31.9% | −53.2% |
| **SPY** (33.3y) | 5 bps | +7.28% | **+9.54%** | 0.49 | **0.52** | −31.5% | −53.0% |
| **SPY** (33.3y) | 10 bps | +7.07% | +9.54% | 0.47 | 0.52 | −31.7% | −53.0% |
| reverse straw man (long summer, cash winter), ^SP500TR, 5 bps | | +4.64% | +10.23% | 0.20 | 0.54 | | |

On both dividend-inclusive tapes the timer **loses on CAGR by ~2.2–2.3 points a year** and
**loses on risk-adjusted terms too** (excess-Sharpe 0.47–0.52 vs 0.52–0.54) — the drawdown cut
(−32% vs −53%) is real, but it's *just less market exposure*, not a Sharpe improvement, because
the summer leg you're avoiding is **positive**, not flat or negative.

**Named artefact:** the same timer run on **price-only ^GSPC + ^IRX** (1960–2026) shows the
*opposite* — timer CAGR **+7.62%** beats buy&hold's **+6.31%**, excess-Sharpe 0.35 vs 0.19. This
is **not evidence the timer works** — it's an artefact of racing a no-dividend equity curve
against a positive cash yield for the summer leg: buy&hold there is missing *all twelve months*
of dividends while the timer is only missing *six*. The moment dividends are put back in (SPY,
^SP500TR above), the advantage reverses. Comparing a price-only benchmark to a cash-substitution
strategy is exactly the kind of apples-to-oranges race the desk's raw-vs-excess-Sharpe rule
exists to catch.

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery is unbiased

Deterministic monthly log-return series, seeded, with a TUNABLE planted winter premium; no
network.

| world | Welch *t* |
|---|--:|
| null (premium = 0), **20 seeds** | mean **−0.01** (sd 1.04), **\|t\| ≥ 2 in 1/20 seeds** (≈ the nominal 5% false-positive rate at a 2σ cutoff — the test is correctly calibrated, not over- or under-powered) |
| planted premium = +40 bps/mo (seed 641) | **+2.38** |

The detector does not systematically fire on the null and recovers a planted premium.
*(A faithful-engine / power check only — never cited in support of the real-tape stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The deep, **price-only** ^GSPC tape (1950–2026, 76 years) clears the desk's
  *t* ≥ 2 bar two ways — Welch **t = +2.78**, Newey-West **t = +2.96** — and its year-block
  bootstrap is decisive (**t = +3.16**, 95% CI [+1.78%, +7.56%], entirely above zero). But the
  **dividend-inclusive** tapes that actually describe a tradable portfolio — ^SP500TR (1988–,
  *t* = +1.33) and SPY (1993–, *t* = +1.10) — **do not clear the bar**, and their year-block
  sign tests are far from significant (*p* = 0.26 / 0.49). A material share of even the
  deep-history result concentrates in **10 crash-adjacent Septembers/Octobers** (1.1% of the
  sample) — pull them out and the deep-tape *t* itself falls below 2 (2.78 → 1.88). The
  Halloween seasonal is real over long, price-only history and the direction is consistent
  everywhere, but this desk's modern, economically correct sample **cannot certify it alone**.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** A Nov→Apr / cash-in-summer timer **trails buy-and-hold on both CAGR
  (by 2.2–2.3 pts/yr) and excess-of-cash Sharpe** on every dividend-inclusive tape tested,
  because May→Oct pays a **positive** ~+3.8–3.9% every six months, not zero. The lower drawdown
  is exposure reduction, not skill. A price-only race makes the timer look like a winner — a
  named artefact of comparing a no-dividend benchmark to a cash-substitution strategy, not a
  real edge.
- **"Driven by a handful of bad Septembers/Octobers?" — CONFIRMED.** Removing the 5 worst
  Septembers and 5 worst Octobers (10/917 months, 1.1% of the sample) cuts the winter-summer
  gap by 35% and drops the deep-history Welch *t* from **+2.78 to +1.88** — below the
  certification bar. The Halloween effect is not a smooth six-month tailwind; it is largely a
  short list of famous crash autumns (1987, 2008, ...) plus a couple of quieter ones (1974,
  1978, 1979, 1986, 2018, 2022).
